Chairwoman Senator Tepler, Chairwoman Representative Hepler and distinguished members
of the committee
My name is Beau Jeffery, age 29, from Windham, Maine. This is my testimony on,LD 336- An
act to change the waiting list system for commercial Lobster and crab fishing license.
I am supportive of LD 336, to make changes the waiting list system that the state currently has
in place. I have worked the decks of lobster boats as a stern-man for 14 years. It has been a life
long dream to captain and own a boat to fish for what our state is known for and built on which is our lobster. With the current system, I don't see how I will live my dreams.
Lobster zone G has 26 people currently on the waiting list with some waiting as long as 15
years. 15 years is an excessive time frame to have to wait to start a career in the lobster and crab industry, after having completed an apprenticeship consisting of 200 days spent at sea, logging
1000 hours over the course of 2 years. With many new regulations and laws being implemented
in recent years I fear wait list times will continue to get longer and inhibit me from getting a
license even more.
Some issues I personally see is that the commissioner will only issue a new license based on the number of renewed license applicants and lobster trap tags purchased each year which
creates inaccuracy within the system.
Some of these inaccuracies include: - Licenses renewed each year by retired fishermen and people who are not actively fishing
whom are still purchasing their maximum amount of tags.
-There are active licensed fishermen purchasing their zones maximum amount of trap tags each year that are not fishing the maximum amount of traps that their zone allows.

This creates inaccurate numbers of active licenses and inaccurate numbers of trap tags in the
states water.

My suggestions for changes for the waitlist system: ~Set a reasonable limit on how long a person waits on the list.

-Implement a limit on how long people who don't fish or who have retired can keep their

license and tags without proof of any landings.

-Give those on the waitlist a reduced amount of tags while on the waiting list so we can keep

everything we learned during our apprenticeships allowing us to work part time until we recieve

our commercial licence and stay up to date onnew laws and regulations.

- Do away with the waiting list system entirely, go to a one out one in system with those who

I
give up their licences.

-Put those who have a suspended lobster license on the back of the list and issue the next

recipient on the wait list that opening.

These changes to the current system could greatly benefit not only those on waiting list

seeking to start their careers in the industry, it would also benefit all aspects of the industry from

lobster buyers, bait dealers, and marine supply shops. It could also boost the economy and

createjobs and tax revenue for the state.

I hope you kindly consider my testimony on these issues and work together and make some

positive changes to thecommercial lobster and crab wait list system.

Thank you, Beau Jeffery

March 6, 2025 - Testimony in support of LD 336: An Act to Change the Waiting List System for Commercial Lobster

Good morning, Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Committee on Marine Resources. I appreciate the chance to speak in support of LD 336, "An Act to Change the Waiting List System for Commercial Lobster and Crab Fishing Licenses."

My name is Representative Billy Bob Faulkingham, and I serve as the House Republican Leader. I
represent House District 12, which includes the towns of Franklin, Gouldsboro, Hancock, Sorrento, Sullivan, Winter Harbor, and Steuben. This legislation proposes a one-to-one entry ratio for lobster licenses, and I believe it is a necessary and fair change for the future of the lobster industry.

The lobster industry is aging rapidly, and the number of young people entering the fishery has declined significantly. Today, more fishermen are over 40 years old than under 40, Ifthe overall number of fishermen in the industry isn't growing, there's no reason to maintain entry ratios above
one-to-one. Keeping these higher ratios creates an unnecessary barrier that prevents hardworking apprentices from gaining full entry into the fishery.
I understand and respect that decisions regarding entry ratios are made at the zone level. However, I believe it's fair to ask: What are the reasons for not adopting a one-to-one ratio? If there are valid concerns, I'd like to hear them. This is a strong and well-managed fishery, and those who have
completed their apprenticeship should be able to access it within a reasonable timeframe.

Creating unnecessary obstacles and prolonged wait times does not strengthen our industry--it weakens it. It discourages young people from pursuing a career on the water, harms our coastal
economy, and undermines the tradition of passing this way of life down to the next generation. Fishermen have always taken pride in mentoring newcomers who have put in the work. If someone
has successfully completed the apprenticeship program and a spot opens up, they should be able to
fish.

I stand before you today as someone who was fortunate enough to enter the fishery before limited
entry was implemented. I did not have to wait on a list-I simply purchased a license and got to work,
just as my father did before me, and his father before him. Knowing that others have been denied
that same opportunity has never sat right with me. To me, this is an issue of fairness.

If today is not the right time to make this change, I can accept that. But I would at least like to understand why. And if a one-to-one ratio is not feasible at this time, I urge the committee to explore ways to encourage zones to consider lowering their ratios.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

Respectfully,

Dear Members of the Maine Marine Resources Committee,
On behalf of the New England Fishermen's Stewardship Association (NEFSA),I am writing to express our strong opposition to LD 336, An Act to Change the Waiting List System for Commercial Lobster and Crab Fishing Licenses. NEFSA represents hundreds of lobstermen
across the State of Maine, advocating for policies that sustain our industry, protect our hardworking fishermen, and ensure the responsible stewardship of our marine resources. Our mission is to uphold the integrity and long~term viability of Maine's lobster fishery by supporting
industry-led management, defending the rights of those who work on the water, and resisting
unnecessary regulatory overreach that threatens the foundation of our coastal communities.
The proposed shift to a 1:1 entry/exit ratio for commercial lobster and crab licenses on a coastwide basis represents a drastic and unwarranted change that would erode the authority and effectiveness of Maine's seven distinct lobster zone councils. These councils were established to ensure that lobster management reflects the unique conditions, traditions, and practices of different regions along Maine's expansive and diverse coastline. Each zone operates under
distinct ecological, economic, and operational challenges, requiring tailored strategies to maintain balance and sustainability within the fishery. The proposed legislation disregards these regional nuances, instead imposing a one-size-fits-all licensing system that would strip local
fishermen of their long~standing role in governing their own fisheries. By centralizing control
and eliminating localized decision-making, LD 336 would undermine a proven, effective system
of fisheries management--one that has been instrumental in preserving Maine's lobster fishery as one of the most sustainable and well-managed in the world.
Furthermore, this proposed shift comes at a time when the lobster industry is already facing an unprecedented series of challenges. The looming prospect of gauge size increases and other resilience measures presents significant concerns, as they could impose additional financial and operational burdens on fishermen who are already struggling to adapt to an unpredictable regulatory environment. The impending right whale regulations set to take effect in 2028bring
further uncertainty, with the potential for sweeping restrictions that could severely impact daily
fishing operations. Additionally, the potential for new tariffs on lobster exports threatens to destabilize our markets, drive down boat prices, and place further economic strain on our fishing communities. With so many complex and pressing issues already weighing heavily on Maine's lobstermen, the last thing our industry needs is a rigid, top-down licensing mandate that disregards the voices of those who know the fishery best.

lt is also critical to consider the changing demographics of Maine's lobstering fleet. In the past year alone, an estimated 400 fishermen gave up their licenses, choosing to exit the fishery altogether. This exodus is not an isolated event but rather part of a broader trend, as Maine's fleet
continues to age and shrink. In the coming years, we can expect a significant number of
additional fishermen to retire, leaving a natural opening for new entrants. A rigid 1:1 entry/exit
system fails to account for this reality and could unnecessarily stifle opportunity for younger generations, discouraging the very succession that is essential to the industry's long-term health. The current zone-based approach allows for more adaptive, localized decision-making, ensuring that entry into the fishery aligns with regional needs rather than an arbitrary statewide quota.
For generations, Maine's lobster industry has been a model of successful, sustainable fisheries management--a testament to the deep commitment, experience, and stewardship of our fishermen. The zone council system has played a critical role in maintaining this balance,
ensuring that local expertise guides regulatory decisions rather than distant, broad-stroke policies that fail to account for the distinct realities of each fishing zone. Preserving this system is essential to maintaining the health of our fishery, the strength of our coastal economies, and the
livelihoods of the countless families who depend on lobstering.
For these reasons, NEFSA strongly urges the committee to reject LD 336 and uphold the
authority of the lobster zone councils, which remain the best mechanism for ensuring
responsible, community~driven fisheries management. We must remain steadfast in protecting
the industry-led approach that has sustained Maine's lobster fishery for generations and reject proposals that would strip fishermen of their right to self-governance.
Thank you for your time, attention, and thoughtful consideration of this critical issue. We
appreciate your commitment to policies that support Maine's hardworking lobstermen and
safeguard the future of this iconic industry.
Sincerely,
Dustin W. Delano Chief Operating Officer
New England Fishermen's Stewardship Association
10036048:
To: Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine Resources From: Emily Coffin, Policy Coordinator Date: March 6th, 2025
Re: LD 336: An Act to Change the Waitlist System for Commercial Lobster and Crab Fishing Licenses
Dear Honorable Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and distinguished members of the Joint Committee on Marine Resources:
The Maine Coast Fishermen's Association (MCFA) is an industry-based nonprofit dedicated to restoring the fisheries of the Gulf of Maine and preserving Maine's iconic fishing communities for future generations. Founded by Maine fishermen to provide a voice in fisheries management, MCFA often advocates for conservation measures in order to protect shared resources.
MCFA is a vocal advocate of accessibility and the encouragement of new entrants to Maine fisheries for the sake of a healthy fishing industry and robust blue economy. We, however, oppose LD 336 because it puts the lobster stock at risk, as it would dramatically increase effort on the population and disadvantage those who are already in the fishery by increasing competition.
Maine lobstermen are known for their dedication to the health of the species they rely upon. The lobster industry has persisted through the years, while other stocks have fluctuated and diminished to an extreme to degree, because of the careful, considerate provisions put in place to maintain the population. As it stands, the current exit ratio for lobster licenses in each zone is such: Zone A (1:3) Zone B (1:3) Zone C (1:1) Zone D (1:5) Zone E (1:5) Zone F (1:5) Zone G (1:5). These ratios were voted on by the respective lobster councils and reflect the needs of each area. By changing the ratio across the board to 1:1, the number of licenses would rise sharply. At a time in which the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission projects a shrinking biomass, it would be unwise and unfair to those presently dependent on the fishery to compete for catch with an influx of new entrants. ASMFC conservation measures such as the increase in gauge size have sparked discontent among those in the fishing industry because it would shrink catch. It is not hard to imagine that a management body such as the commission might react with more controversial and conservatory measures in response to a surge in lobster licenses and effort on the stock. This would further divide this industry and put undue stress upon fishing families and communities.
An uptick in lobster licenses would also mean an uptick of ropes in the water. Firstly, this is an issue for areas with high gear density. Many bays along the coast are filled to the brim with traps and have little room for added strings of traps or even singles. Adding an influx of licenses and traps to crowded bays would be a recipe for competition and animosity amongst those in the industry.
Secondly, adding lines to the water would further set back the state's goals to remove rope from the water in accordance with Right Whale protection rules and regulations. Ropes are the reason that the federal government attempted to shut down the lobster fishery because of the potential danger they pose to the endangered whales. The fishery and the state are still in limbo as on-demand lobster gear is tested and developed by the few who are willing. State regulators and fishermen alike cannot afford to add more traps than necessary into the mix.

All this being said, the pressures on the industry, both social, economic, and regulatory, are immense. Adding effort to the fishery would negatively affect those financially dependent on lobster and the resilience of the industry as a whole. The exit ratios were determined and voted on by the Zone Councils which are entrusted to make the best decisions for their constituents. MCFA believes that the current ratios are satisfactory to a healthy expansion of the fishery and protection of the resource, of which we all depend greatly upon.
Thank you, Emily Coffin, Policy Coordinator Maine Coast Fishermen's Association

Against

March 6, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Marine Resources Committee, my name is Jarod Bray. i am the Board Chairman of the Maine Lobstermen's Association (MLA). The MLA opposes LD
336 to change the exit ratio for any lobster zone waiting list to one to one.
The MLA is a strong advocate for the zone council process. It was created to give lobstermen a voice in
local management, in partnership with the Department of Marine Resources (DMR) and the Legislature, to address local issues in the lobster fishery along the Maine coast. This co-management process is unique and has successfully maintained a sustainable and profitable fishery.
At times, the lobster zone exit ratios have been controversial because the wait lists in certain zones became very long. However, the exit ratios have played an important role in reducing effort in the fishery, which has also reduced the amount of rope in the water and the risk the fishery poses to right
whales.
Many believed that the waiting lists would work themselves out given the high average age of lobstermen in the fishery. It appears that this transition is now happening. At the January Lobster
Advisory Council meeting, the Commissioner reported that approximately 250 licenses were retired
from the lobster fishery in 2024. DMR also reports that waiting lists have shrunk dramatically and wait
times to get into the fishery are decreasing across all lobster zones.
The southwestern part of the state has had some of the longest waiting lists. At its recent meeting in January, the Zone F Council discussed gathering input from zone lobstermen to consider lowering its exit ratio. The Zone G Council has not yet formally met yet this year, but lobstermen have begun informal discussions on lowering the exit ratio. As increasing numbers of licenses have been retired, lobstermen are far less concerned that zones are overcrowded and have become more focused on the need to
preserve future fishing opportunities for their communities.
If LD 336 were to pass, it would significantly limit input from the zone councils and increase the number of lobstermen and traps in each zone. More traps in the water could lead to reduced profitability for
each lobsterman since landings are currently in decline, and more stringent whale rules. The MLA
strongly urges the Committee to vote ought not to pass on LD 336.
Thank you for your consideration.

TESTIMONY OF
Patrick Keliher
Department of Marine Resources
The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying
in Opposition to
LD 336 An Act to Change the Waiting List System for Commercial Lobster and Crab Fishing Licenses Before the Committee on Marine Resources Sponsored by Representative Bagshaw Date of Hearing: March 6, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Hepler, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Marine
Resources, my name is Patrick Keliher, I am the Commissioner of the Department of Marine Resources, and I am testifying on behalf of the Department in opposition to LD 336.
The lobster zone councils were created 30 years ago, to facilitate a co-management approach for local and regional management of Maine's lobster fishery. At the time of their creation, the Zones were vested by the Legislature with three items that they may propose to the commissioner to place limitations on the lobster and crab fishing license holders that fish in that zone. These were: the number of lobster traps fished, the number of lobster traps allowed on a trawl, and the time of day when lobster fishing may occur. These authorities were subsequently expanded when lobster became a limited entry fishery in 1999 to allow Zone Councils to also recommend the exit ratio for their Zone and, subsequent to that, whether that annual calculation should be based on licenses not renewed or trap tags retired. An exit ratio is defined by the amount of effort that must leave the Zone before a new license is created.
LD 336 would eliminate one of the authorities that a zone holds, eliminating their ability to recommend a ratio to the Department, leaving only one possible ratio for all Zones, which would be 1:1. For reference, the existing ratios that have been recommended by each Zone and adopted through the
regulatory process are currently as follows:
Zone A: One license awarded for every three licenses retired (3:1) Zone B: One license awarded for every three licenses retired (3:1) Zone C: One license awarded for every license retired (1:1) Zone D: One license awarded for every 4000 tags retired (5:1 with tags) Zone E: One license awarded for every five licenses retired (5:1) Zone F: One license awarded for every 4000 tags retired (5:1 with tags) Zone G: One license awarded for every 4000 tags retired (5:1 with tags)
It is worth noting that in recent years there has been a trend toward more lobster licenses being retired, which has resulted in larger numbers of licenses being issued in nearly every Zone. Please see the table below for the supporting data:

As you can see from both the ratios and the licenses authorized, the eastern Zones tend to be more permissive with regard to issuing more licenses, while the western zones have selected ratios that are more conservative. However, at their most recent meeting in January, the Zone F Council requested information on the current license and tag trends in their Zone, and discussed the potential to initiate the process to amend their current ratio to something less conservative, such as 3 licenses retired for 1 license issued. This process begins with a survey of all license holders in the Zone, which the Council may choose to initiate at their next meeting.
Since the development of the waiting lists, there has often been frustration from those on the waiting list about the amount oftime they must spend on the list before being offered a license. At the direction of this committee, the Department has regularly gone back to the Zone Councils and shared the concerns expressed by some legislators about wait times for certain Zones. However, the Zone Councils have typically maintained the ratios they previously put in place.
l would urge the committee to think about this issue beyond a waiting list. As you are all aware, the lobster industry faces more, very onerous, whale regulations and a 1:1 exit ratio will result in more
licenses and more endlines, at a time we need to be looking at ways to reduce risk to endangered right
whales.
If the Legislature wants to override the authority previously granted to the Zones, the Department would urge you to closely review the current waiting lists and length of time that prospective license
holders have been waiting, to determine if a "one size fits all" solution is actually warranted. We have
attached the current Zone waiting lists for your information.
Ultimately, the issues associated with access to licenses in all of Maine's fisheries are some of the most difficult with which to grapple. There is no "right" answer, as we always discussing how to allocate
access to limited resources. Increasing that access impacts existing license holders. Decisions about
how and when to expand access to licenses should be made with consideration of many factors,
including trends in the resource, and external forces that could impact the fishery going forward, such as the pending risk reductions for the protection of right whales. For these reasons, the Department does not support a blanket application of a 1:1 ratio in every Zone.
Thank you for your consideration and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
